heroText: Asmara is Eritrea's highland capital, a UNESCO World Heritage city famous for its well-preserved Italian Art Deco and modernist architecture. First-time visitors should see the striking Fiat Tagliero Building shaped like an airplane, browse the National Museum of Eritrea for archaeology and ethnography, and sip espresso along Harnet Avenue at one of the city's classic Italian-era cafes. Asmara International Airport lies northeast of the centre, a short drive from most hotels.

areas.name: City centre (Harnet Avenue)
areas.text: The city centre along Harnet Avenue holds most of Asmara's Art Deco landmarks, cafes and hotels, the best base for walking tours.

areas.name: Tiravolo
areas.text: Tiravolo is a quieter residential district close to the centre, offering a calmer base within easy reach of downtown sights.

areas.name: Gejeret
areas.text: Gejeret is a growing residential area on the city's edge, useful for longer stays away from the busiest central streets.

airports.name: Asmara International Airport (ASM)
airports.text: Asmara International Airport is about 7 kilometres northeast of the city centre; taxis are available for the short transfer into town.

airportTransfer.value: Compare road transfer time between Asmara International Airport (ASM) and central Asmara before choosing an airport-area or city-centre hotel.

stayOverview: Base in the city centre along Harnet Avenue for walking access to Asmara's Art Deco landmarks and cafes. Tiravolo and Gejeret offer quieter, more residential alternatives within easy reach of downtown.
hotelIntro: Most visitors stay in the city centre near Harnet Avenue for walking access to the cathedral, cafes and Art Deco buildings, while Tiravolo and Gejeret suit travellers wanting a calmer, more residential base.
rentalCars: A rental car isn't necessary for compact, walkable central Asmara, though a hired driver helps for trips beyond the capital.

travelTips.title: Best base
travelTips.text: Stay near Harnet Avenue in the city centre for walking access to Asmara's Art Deco landmarks and classic cafes.

travelTips.title: Photography permits
travelTips.text: Check current rules on photographing government buildings and infrastructure, since restrictions in Eritrea can be stricter than in neighbouring countries.

travelTips.title: Cafe culture
travelTips.text: Set aside time for a coffee at one of Asmara's Italian-era cafes, a signature part of the city's daily rhythm.

travelTips.title: Visa and travel
travelTips.text: Arrange visas and any required travel permits well ahead of time, since independent travel rules for Eritrea can change with little notice.

nearbyIdeas.name: Massawa
nearbyIdeas.label: City
nearbyIdeas.text: Massawa, Eritrea's historic Red Sea port, is a scenic descent from Asmara down the escarpment and a striking contrast in climate and architecture.

nearbyIdeas.name: Keren
nearbyIdeas.label: City
nearbyIdeas.text: Keren, Eritrea's second-largest city, is known for its camel market and colonial-era buildings, a worthwhile day trip from Asmara.

history.label: Origins
history.text: According to Eritrean Tigrinya oral traditional history, there were four clans living in the Asmera area on the Kebessa Plateau: the Gheza Gurtom, the Gheza Shelele, the Gheza Serenser and Gheza Asmae.

The first mention of Asmara comes from a Latin itinerary during the reign of Emperor Dawit I (1382–1411). Italian Asmara Asmara, a small village in the nineteenth century, started to grow quickly when it.
Governor Ferdinando Martini made it the capital city of Italian Eritrea in 1897.

history.label: 20th century
history.text: In the early 20th century, the Eritrean Railway was built to the coast, passing through the town of Ghinda, under the direction of Carlo Cavanna.
In both 1913 and 1915 the city suffered only slight damage in large earthquakes.

history.label: 1930s
history.text: By the late 1930s, Asmara was called Piccola Roma (Little Rome).
The city was home to the US Army's Kagnew Station installation from 1943 until 1977.
The Eritrean War of Independence began in 1961 and ended in 1991, resulting in the independence of Eritrea.

history.label: Growth
history.text: These villages were frequently attacked by clans from the lowlands, until the women of each clan decided that to preserve peace the four clans must unite.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: The Kingdom of Italy invested in the industrial development of Asmara (and surrounding areas of Eritrea), but the beginning of World War II brought this to a halt.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: During the Federation, Asmara was no longer the capital city.

history.label: Regional role
history.text: After independence, Asmara again became the capital of Eritrea.
